raw_comment:
My first impression of the graph was that I noticed the amount of men's participation in the labor force has declined in every country depicted from 1980-2015.While there are periods of increase for each country, they all show a downward, negative trend. I would attribute this to the diminishing influence of gender roles since the 80's. Women's increased involvement in the work force has reduced the availability of jobs for men, who previously dominated most working positions.

The most significant decrease is in the United States. This could be attributed, also, to issues of unemployment that have been prevalent in our nation. While the graph is inclusive of men actively seeking work, discouragement or difficulty finding feasible, well-paid, hiring positions as a result of increased competition could attribute to this decrease. Issues of retirement could also explain this decrease, as much of the baby-boomer generation is exiting the work force. 

I wonder why the labor-force participation in Japan is significantly higher than that of in other countries. I read an article last year that explained Japan's issues of aging population; they have a large population of people over 60, or retirement age, that are refusing to retire and remain in the workforce. This is why much of the younger generation, recent graduates, are failing to find positions in the workforce. I wonder if this information impacts Japan's male employment.

raw_comment:
The first thing I notice when I look at this graph is that the percentage of men seeking work or actively working is much lower in recent years in the United States compared to the other countries represented on the graph. This may imply that men are having difficulties in trying to get jobs or imply issues with our education system (the cost of going to college, etc.) I also notice that the sharpest decline for the United States on the graph occurred when the recession of 2008 hit, which makes sense. 

I wonder why  Japan has such a consistently high labor force rate compared to all other countries- even countries with traditionally very high qualities of life, like Denmark. I also wonder why the United States experienced another drop from around 2010-2015, and then why we are experiencing growth again. Some research could provide me with these answers. 

The deeper story behind this graph is that the United States is behind other developed countries in the percentage of men who are either working or actively seeking work, despite all of the countries in the graph being part of the Organisation for economic cooperation and development, which is supposed to promote sustainable economic growth by sharing strategies. For some reason, the United States doesn’t seem to be implementing these strategies.

raw_comment:
Aha! Serious social trends! Here we go...
I can see how labor participation rate among men aged 25-54 has been changing since 80' in 7 countries. Negative trends in general, somewhere stronger, somewhere weaker. Good looking datavis. I have an immediate impression US is in bad situation (low position, strong descending slope). But hold on...

Let's wonder about:
1) Why these 7 countries are presented here? Highest participation in 80' or what? (rather not exactly - no Korea, Sweden, Spain or Australia, if I checked OECD source correctly) By the way, why do the time series start from 1980?
2) Why Y axis minimum is set to 87% and makes US change horribly drastic? Is 88% a reason to really worry about?
3) What is an exact definition of "working" etc (e.g. 2 hours every week counts?) and is it comparable across different countries / in one country in time (almost 40 years of stats are included here)?
4) Why men 25-54? + What is retirement age in selected countries? Curious to see trends for woman as well (checked them, interesting indeed)
5) Why the trend is negative in general? Common hidden process? This question leads to a storytelling part.

Suppose my methodology worries were unjustified and everything is perfect.  Less % of people are working! Economic recession or global structural / cultural? Should US worry? There is small uptick at the US line, so maybe it will rebound and not sink. 

Got interested in this column, so tried to follow. Thanks for datavis stimulation :)

I do not know how they gathered this information or if it was through a survey, but I know that if unemployed people are asked if they are unemployed, they would rather say they are "looking for work" than admitting they are not working. This may produce bias depending on how the information was gathered.

raw_comment: Something I noticed about this graph is the source's choice to graph and present the data using only  around the top decile in the y axis. This makes the rates seem to drop more significantly when seen visually without looking at the actual numbers.  To this effect, the difference of labor participation rates between various countries appear to be larger than they actually are. I wonder what other confounding factors affect the data from this representation, such as recessions or times of war. Although there is a general negative correlation for all countries, they all experience up-and-down movement, which could relate to the country's economic status in recession or recovery. With these things in mind, this graph seems to show the resilience of each country's workforce in putting people into work as others leave, retire, or die. However, it does show the effects of recession on labor force participation, as seen in the US around 2008.

raw_comment:
The most evident point that the graph illustrates is the fact that labor force participation rate for men has declined and is lower now than in the '80s. Japan has and always had the highest percentage of people in the labor force, US currently has the lowest. I think the graph tells the story of the different cultures of different countries. Speaking generally, the school leaving age has increased. Now, people need to get more amount of education to get a sufficiently paying job than before. Since the graph illustrates the participation rate of only men, it can also tell us something about the change in people's attitudes about gender roles. A greater number of women are now a part of the labor force and more men are taking up responsibilities traditionally deemed as those of women (stay at home dads, for example). The economic development in the countries is very high, therefore I don't think that the declining labor force participation rate is necessarily a problem, in fact the countries may be heading in the right direction with the change in attitudes. 

I do wonder why Japan has the highest rate and if it is a good thing. Japan has a lower women's labor force participation rate than the United States as of 2016, and this may call for a change. Also, the sharp plummet and the following increase in Germany participation rate may tell an interesting story.

raw_comment:
It seems we were all disappointed that the U. S. fell so far behind the other countries in labor-force participation rate, especially behind Japan.  We also puzzled at why for most of 1980 - 2017, the rate was declining for all countries.  The reasons most frequently mentioned were technology replacing workers, women working rather than men, and Americans not as motivated to work.  Some said that jobs have been lost to other countries and Americans are staying in school longer.  The graph shows where the data came from:  Alan Kreuger of Princeton University.
